name: Bioenergetic diet
lead: The bioenergetic diet, also called the Ray Peat diet, is an eating approach built around the idea that supporting cellular energy production and metabolic rate improves health and appearance. Followers emphasize easily digested carbohydrates such as fruit, honey and juice, along with dairy and shellfish, and they limit polyunsaturated fats.

Within looksmaxxing and strength circles, practitioners say it supports leaner, fuller-looking physiques, better skin and warmth. On T Nation, one member described a high-carbohydrate plan of fruit and honey alongside beef as 'the bioenergetic view'.[1] The approach originates with biologist Ray Peat; no clinical trials of the diet as a package are known.

chain: Followers report higher metabolic rate and energy
Leaner, fuller physique and better skin (claimed)
angle.text: Followers eat fruit, honey, dairy and shellfish and avoid polyunsaturated oils, aiming to raise metabolism. They claim leaner body composition, clearer skin and more energy as a result.

infobox: Fruit, honey, dairy, low polyunsaturated fat

paras: The diet centers on carbohydrate from fruit, honey and juice, with protein from dairy, shellfish and beef and a deliberate reduction of polyunsaturated fats. Members of the T Nation forum have discussed the 'bioenergetic view' while trying high-fruit, high-honey eating alongside beef.[1]
Forum posts discuss polyunsaturated fats, including omega-3s, as damaging through oxidation, a position raised in a T Nation thread where the poster said they were not necessarily in agreement.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation the diet is discussed as an alternative approach to carbs and fats.[1]

claims.claim: Eating lots of fruit and honey raises metabolism and improves body composition
claims.believers: A poster reports eating 15-20 lbs of fruit and 1-1.5 pints of honey weekly while cutting calories slightly.[1]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this diet as a whole.

claims.claim: Omega-3 fats are more damaging than omega-6 fats because they oxidize readily
claims.believers: A forum thread argued EPA, DHA and ALA are highly susceptible to oxidation.[2]
claims.experts: No published trials have tested this claim; it is presented in the forum as a debate topic.
